content: Fungal infections of the feet typically affect the outermost layer of the skin, known as the epidermis. These infections frequently occur between the toes, causing symptoms such as pain and itchiness. When fungal infections involve the toenails, a condition called onychomycosis, the entire nail plate can be affected. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of topical treatments in curing fungal infections of the skin and nails of the feet, as well as their ability to prevent recurrence. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to January 2005. Additional sources, such as the Science Citation Index and other bibliographies, were also reviewed. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants with fungal infections of the skin and nails of the foot that were confirmed through mycological diagnosis. Two independent authors summarized the included trials and assessed the quality of their reporting using a structured data extraction tool. Out of 144 identified studies, 67 trials met the inclusion criteria. Placebo-controlled trials demonstrated the following pooled risk ratios (RR) for treatment failure in skin infections: Allylamines: RR 0.33 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.44) Azoles: RR 0.30 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.45) Ciclopiroxolamine: RR 0.27 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.66) Tolnaftate: RR 0.19 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.44) Butenafine: RR 0.33 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.45) Undecanoates: RR 0.29 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.70) A meta-analysis of 11 trials comparing allylamines and azoles revealed a risk ratio for treatment failure of RR 0.63 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.94) in favor of allylamines, indicating that allylamines were slightly more effective than azoles in treating skin infections. Evidence regarding the treatment of fungal infections of the toenails was more limited. Ciclopiroxolamine and butenafine were found to be effective, but both require daily application for extended periods, often at least one year. Among the six trials focusing on nail infections, ciclopiroxolamine demonstrated poor cure rates, while amorolfine appeared to be significantly more effective. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings. In conclusion, placebo-controlled trials consistently show that allylamines and azoles are significantly more effective than placebo in treating athlete's foot. Allylamines are slightly more effective than azoles and are now available over the counter (OTC). However, additional research is necessary to better understand the efficacy of antifungal agents for treating nail infections.
